subject: Computer Networking
title: Why Networks Get Attacked
description: Learn Why Networks Get Attacked in one minute.

hook.text: Every device online is a potential target. Hackers don't need a reason — they need an opening.

buildup.text: Motivations vary: money, espionage, activism, or just curiosity. Different attackers have different goals.

discovery.text: Most attacks are automated. Bots scan millions of IPs looking for known vulnerabilities. No one is specifically chosen.

twist.text: Small businesses think they're too small to target. But bots don't care about size — they care about open ports.

climax.text: The cost of cybercrime is estimated at $10 trillion annually. It's the biggest transfer of wealth in history.

punchline.text: If it's connected, it's a target. Size doesn't matter.

quiz.question: How do most network attacks begin?
options: Automated bots scanning for known vulnerabilities

details.summary: Networks are attacked for financial gain, espionage, activism, and disruption. Cybercriminals target valuable data like credit cards and intellectual property, nation-states seek intelligence, and hacktivists pursue ideological goals. Every connected network is a potential target regardless of size.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding attacker motivations helps prioritize defenses. The most damaging attacks target what matters most to your organization, not just what is technically easiest to exploit.
takeaways: Financial gain drives the majority of cyberattacks today
Every network is a target regardless of organization size
Understanding attacker goals helps prioritize defensive measures

faq.question: Are small businesses really targets for cyberattacks?
faq.answer: Small businesses are frequent targets because they often have weaker security than large enterprises. Automated attacks scan the entire internet indiscriminately.

faq.question: What are the most common types of network attacks?
faq.answer: Phishing, ransomware, and business email compromise are the most common. Automated scanning and exploitation of known vulnerabilities target unpatched systems. DDoS attacks disrupt services. Supply chain attacks compromise trusted software to reach many targets at once.
